global.headline: AfD takes Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as Merz's CDU collapses to fifth
summary: Exit polls put the AfD first in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on 38 per cent, with Friedrich Merz's CDU at or below the 5 per cent threshold for representation — the party's worst state result since 9 per cent in Bremen in 1951. “It is a disaster,” Merz said. “The CDU got crushed in the polarisation between the SPD and the AfD.”

In Berlin the same day, Die Linke led on 26 per cent and the AfD came fourth on 13.5 per cent, up from 9.1 per cent in 2023 — two weeks after it took 44 per cent in Saxony-Anhalt. Alice Weidel said the CDU cannot continue with Merz; he vowed to press on with economic reform.
global.geopolitical: A second AfD state win in a fortnight makes a far-right Land government arithmetically real and leaves the chancellor who anchors Germany's Ukraine and defence-spending positions visibly weakened before this week's UN General Assembly.
global.socioeconomic: Merz staked his chancellorship on unpopular economic reform. A party polling near the threshold in an eastern state has little authority left to impose the labour and spending changes he says Germany needs.

global.headline: United Russia wins as Ukraine's largest drone attack hits Moscow
summary: Initial Central Election Commission data gave United Russia 57.5 per cent as three days of voting closed, on turnout of 56.66 per cent; final results are not due before 25 September. It is the first Duma election since the invasion; Yabloko, the only registered anti-war party, was barred last month.

Ukraine meanwhile mounted its largest attack on the capital region. Russia's defence ministry said it downed over 1,900 drones, bombs and missiles; Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 were downed near Moscow, but some reached the Gazprom Neft refinery at Kapotnya and one hit a residential block. Three were killed in the Moscow region and 20 injured. Zelensky spoke to Trump and agreed to meet in New York.
global.geopolitical: Kyiv timed the strike to the vote and Sobyanin said so. Zelensky goes to New York with the refinery campaign as his only live leverage, days after Trump signed the Russia sanctions law.
global.socioeconomic: Kapotnya is among Russia's largest refineries by volume. Striking refining rather than export terminals squeezes domestic fuel supply and the receipts Zelensky called “billions that sustain the war machine”.

global.headline: Iran warns of a new US campaign as Houthis press toward Marib
summary: Iran's military command said on Sunday, via Tasnim, that it had information the US and regional partners may be preparing fresh action, and warned that any attack would bring sustained strikes on US bases and on any state that assists. No US strikes have been reported in over two weeks.

Trump told Fox News he was in “deciding mode”, naming a deal, more economic pressure or military action as the paths. He said Washington remains in contact with the Houthis and will not enter their war with Saudi Arabia. The State Department warned of rapid escalation, the Riyadh embassy barred travel to Taif and Yanbu, and Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca while advancing on Marib and Taiz.
global.geopolitical: Tehran's warning extends liability to any host or helper, aimed at the Gulf states that base US aircraft and at Seoul, which refused a Hormuz deployment two days earlier. It arrives as Pezeshkian flies to New York.
global.socioeconomic: Markets reopen on Monday having last settled Brent at US$103.87 on Friday, now against a threatened new campaign, US travel curbs on Yanbu, and a Houthi advance on Marib's gas fields that no one has priced.

global.headline: US and China open talks on AI, tariffs and critical minerals
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice-Premier He Lifeng began an all-day session at JPMorgan Chase's Manhattan headquarters on Sunday morning, with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer taking part, to prepare deliverables for the Trump-Xi summit in Washington on 24 September. The agenda is artificial intelligence, tariffs and critical minerals. A senior US official said on Friday that China's performance on critical minerals “has not been up to par” and would be raised.
global.geopolitical: Beijing arrives with leverage it did not have in July: Araghchi visited last week, and China's exemption from designation over Iranian crude purchases is still unresolved. A minerals deliverable would buy room on everything else.
global.socioeconomic: Critical-minerals access is the binding constraint on US defence and battery manufacturing. An AI chapter would be the first time American export controls are negotiated with Beijing rather than simply imposed on it.

global.headline: White House drafts an order giving a board veto over NIH grants
summary: White House officials met on Friday to draft an executive order creating an external committee empowered to veto National Institutes of Health grant awards that do not conform to the administration's priorities. The board would include NIH director Jay Bhattacharya and budget chief Russell Vought and would have to decide unanimously.

The meeting was contentious. Vought accused Bhattacharya of funding work at odds with administration priorities, including diversity-related research, and Trump asked him to cut Harvard's funding, which he refused. The order would build on a 400-page proposal published earlier this year that de-emphasises peer review and widens political appointees' latitude to terminate grants at will.
global.geopolitical: American biomedical funding sets the direction of global research. A political veto over what may be studied hands a recruiting argument to European and Chinese institutions already courting US researchers.
global.socioeconomic: A unanimity rule lets any one member block an award. The damage starts before any grant is refused: multi-year trials and the university posts built around them stall at the point where funding stops looking predictable.

singapore.headline: Solar saved Singapore S$123.8m in fuel import costs, report finds
summary: Solar investment saved Singapore an estimated S$123.8 million (US$97 million) in power-related fossil fuel imports over five months earlier this year, after the Strait of Hormuz crisis drove energy prices up, according to a Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air report published in late August. Nearly all of it came from avoided gas imports, about S$51 million (US$40 million) of that from escaping the Hormuz premium on gas. CREA's Isaac Levi called them modelled wholesale-price estimates.

The same report found Singapore still incurred about S$10.3 billion (US$8.1 billion) in additional gross fossil fuel costs in the six months after the war began, 13th among 171 territories behind China, India and the United States.
singapore.geopolitical: The figure puts a price on what Hormuz costs an economy that imports all its fuel, and strengthens the case Singapore is making regionally for interconnection — the Keppel cable to Riau solar, licensed this month, rests on the same argument.
singapore.socioeconomic: The saving is roughly one per cent of the extra import bill. At current scale solar blunts a price shock rather than absorbing it, which is the argument for storage and imports rather than panels alone.

singapore.headline: Haze eases as every region returns to moderate air quality
summary: The central region's 24-hour PSI left the unhealthy band at 7pm on 20 September, reading 100 after 120 at 10am, and 95 by 11pm; it had been unhealthy since 1pm the day before. The west peaked at 106 at 10am and fell to 91, the east entered the unhealthy range at 3am with 102 and fell to 75, and the north (68) and south (71) stayed moderate throughout. Hourly PM2.5 was back in the normal band across the island by 9pm. The National Environment Agency still forecasts moderate to unhealthy readings, with dry conditions persisting over Sumatra and Kalimantan.
singapore.geopolitical: A second unhealthy episode this month, from fires in another country, and again nothing follows. Transboundary haze returns to the ASEAN agenda each burning season with no enforcement mechanism attached to it.
singapore.socioeconomic: The cost lands before any advisory does — on hawkers, outdoor diners and construction crews who lose a day either way. NEA's forecast of continued dry weather means it recurs rather than passes.

singapore.headline: Three new bus services planned for Tengah, Choa Chu Kang, Woodlands
summary: Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said at Tengah Community Club on 20 September that three new services are planned, and that shuttle buses shadowing the Jurong Region Line will run from the second half of 2027 until the trains start from mid-2028. Tengah has gone from about 12,000 residents a year ago to 28,000, and is projected to reach 57,000 within two years.

Services in the town have grown from four in May 2025 to 11. Siow said he chose more connections over more buses per route; peak-only services can be extended if off-peak demand appears. The Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme has added or extended 37 services and improved 76, serving over 300,000 commuters a day.
singapore.geopolitical: No external dimension; this is domestic transport policy.
singapore.socioeconomic: Tengah's population doubles again before its MRT line opens, so buses carry the gap for two years. Running peak-only services first rations a shortage of drivers rather than of buses, and that is the constraint to watch.

singapore.headline: New guidelines give delivery riders condo parking bays and lockers
summary: Riders welcomed guidelines issued by the Land Transport Authority and Urban Redevelopment Authority recommending dedicated parking bays and collection points in condominiums and malls. One rider told The Straits Times she parks her e-bike on public paths and risks a fine because the walk to a doorstep can take eight minutes, and that when customers do not answer the intercom she waits outside or tailgates a resident.

Experts and condominium managers said cost, security and residents' expectations will decide take-up. Older and smaller developments have no space to reallocate, while new projects can design the facilities in from the planning stage.
singapore.geopolitical: No external dimension; this is domestic labour and land-use policy.
singapore.socioeconomic: Recommendations, not rules: the burden shifts to management councils that pay for the bays and to residents asked to accept strangers at their blocks. Riders' unpaid waiting time is the cost this would recover, and no one is currently billed for it.

word.definition: Inclined to break apart into factions; reproducing by splitting.
word.etymology: From Latin fissus, “split”, and parere, “to bring forth”; coined in 1830s biology for organisms that reproduce by division.
word.example: A fissiparous electorate left Merz's CDU near the 5 per cent threshold, crushed between the AfD and the SPD.
